than the American coIOrs.

forfeiture. or a fine not exceeding $500,
while the American laws provide absolute
forfeiture. He says if vessel has a
medium cargo she can well afford to pay a

profit.

British schooners prepare to discharge
their white crews, man their vessels with
Indians and go to Boring Sea. 1t appears
under these conditions the British sealers
have some kind of assurance that they
will be amply protected.

ciate the deprivations you have undergone

tomorrow the entire brigade will move
from Weston on to Washington on foot.
call for provisions was issued late this

men, who alternately cheered for General
Kelly and called out subscriptions for his
commissary. Before the meeting had ad-
journed sufficient food for several days

teams to transport II were provided.


Kelly informed his meD tonight that the

but he has not fully decided on his route.

routes across the State, but possibly his
entire army will move en- masse. What

expect transportation, subsistence and

night was the only demonstration of i'm
portance which has occurred since Satur-

pared with the feverish uncertainty and
threatening aspect which marked the pre-
vious twenty-four hours. Kelly remained

knots Of men gathered about the streets of

situation, but no attempts to intercept
trains were made, and the marching col
umns Of angry men of yesterday were
minus. On every hand sympathy for

deuunciatlon of the railroad companies

monster demonstration has been arranged

There ere few things more disagree
able than to put on a pair Of stiff. brittle
shoes that have been thrown aside 10
dry after rainy day. Here is formula
that claims to eradicate the trouble:
First wipe Off gently with a soft cloth
all surface water and mud: then. while
still wet. rub well with paraffine oil,
using flannel for the purpose. Set them
aside till partially dry, when a second
treatment with oil is advisable. They
may then be deposited in a conveniently
warm place. where they will dry grad
ually and thoroughly. Before applying
French kid dressing give them a final
rubbing with the flannel still slightly
dampened with paraffine and the boots
will be soft and flexible as new kid and
be very little affected by their bath in
the rain.

A fierce battle for life between large
spider and wasp was witnessed by
Fifteenth ward man in his garden one
day last summer. The spider had spread
her web in a corner of the fence and
was patiently waiting for something to
turn up. Suddenly a wasp flew into the
web. He was firmly caught, but his des-
perate efforts to escape tore several holes
in the fimsy network about him. Here
the spider rushed out and rapidly be-
gan to repair the breaks. The wasp
fought harder still and seemed to be
trying to get chance to sting his sly
foe.


In minute or two the wasp lay per-
fectly still, as if dead. The spider
rushed out and seized the body Of her
victim. The wasp, who had apparently
been playing possum, suddenly became
very much alive, and in flash spider
and wasp were clasped in death lock.
There was short, fierce struggle, and
both insects fell from the dilapidated
web to the ground. They lay there quite
still, and the interested spectator, stoop
ing over them, found that both were
dead. -Philadelphia Record.

The steamer City of Picking, which ar
rived at San Francisco on Saturday from
China and Japan. by way of Honolulu. was
caught in a typhoon Off the coast of Japan
on November % and was all but wrecked.
A wave smashed her deck houses and three
lifeboats.


The Picking had been having bad weather
all that morning, and Capt. Searle remained
on the bridge until noon, when he went aft
to his state room. leaving the first officer
in charge of the vessel Luncheon was be-
ing prepared, and the children were already
In the dining room at their monday meal.
when about 1920 o'clock huge wave was
seen coming toward the ship on the star
board beam. The first officer gave orders
to bring the steamer around, but the i'm
mense wave was travelling with lightning
speed. 1t struck the steamer abaft the main
rigging. The shock was terrific


Five lifeboats were torn from the davits
and hurled along the deck. The water
poured over the ship and into the cabin and
dining saloon flooding everything. The sky
light over the engine room was ashed
and the engine room deluged with tons of
water The lifeboats were swept down the
deck into the deck saloon, and that struc-
ture and Capt Searle's cabin were mashed
into bits and the wreckage was carried into





was carried away and then the sides fol-
lowed. Capt. Searle was caught in the de-
bris and carried into the starboard SOUP
pers. bruised and bleeding. A panic ensued
among the passengers. Several men and
women had been hurt.
The stewardess was in the dining saloon
with the children, and her first care was to
protect the little ones. As soon as she had
them in a safe place she went to the assist
ance of the women. The officers and pas
sengers went to the aid of the captain, and
extricated him from his perilous position
not a moment too soon, for scarcely min
ute after he had been rescued the saloon
plano was dashed to pieces right on the spot
where he had been thrown.


In the cabin the water was waist deep,
and in the engine room Chief Engineer
Stewart and his men were up to their necks
In water. The fate of the ship depended
on these men, and. although they knew that
another sea meant the laundering of the

thousands of pounds. Many buildings

Sitka on June 10. when the wages were
paid. The Indians then lowered their
canoes and prepared to desert the ship.
living to new regulations Indians are
the only available hunters for the
Behring Sea. White men cannot use

numbered twenty-one, while the captain
had only five white men and two faith
full Indians to help him. The Indians
threatened to scuttle the vessel, secur-
ing the skins which were in the hold

owing to their bad management.


At last the captain and his men got
the drop on, the mutineers and drove
them Into the hold, where they shut
them up. He then sailed for Sitka,
where he obtained handouts from the
Government officials and brought the
Indians down in irons.

story of their experience:


The Ethiopia struck the iceberg on the
afternoon Of the 9Th, while she was steam

terrific. Everybody who was standing at
the moment of impact was thrown to the
floor. At first the officers feared that the
vessel would not float, and the captain or
dered that the boats be lowered.


The excited passengers crowded up to the
deck, most Of the women weeping and the
men asking many questions. The pumps
were lowered just after the captain or
dered down the boats, but no water was
found In the hold. The order for the boats
was then countermanded and something
like confidence was restored among the
passengers.


Soon the fog lifted. As there was little
sea the crew Were able TO work to advan-
tage in making temporary repairs. wall
OF bags OF Hour was built up near tho bow.
When the flour had become thoroughly sat
urated IL was almost as hard and unfolding
cement The crew worked for two days
shifting the cargo aft so as TO lift the
broken part of the bow above the water.
The Ethiopia, which had been stopped for
repairs was put ahead after the worst dam
aged portion Of her bow had been partially
closed and braced. AT first she went at
quarter speed, then at three-quarters and
after passing Tory Island at full speed.


Nobody aboard the Ethiopia was injured.
and the cargo was not greatly damaged.
Persons who saw the Ethiopias bow yes
terday marvel that she was kept afioat
after the collision. That the vessel was
saved they think was due to the stability

agement OF the captain.


The passengers were so pleased with the
untiring and successful efforts of the crew

encounter with the slavers.
1t was stated that landing parties from

dealer, who had been carrying off into
bondage and severely illtreating the help
less natives of a number of villages along
that part of the coast which he rules over.

PRINCETON. ILL.,, Aug. 22-The Illinois
and Mississippi canal, commonly known
as the Hennepin canal. has been brought
into prominence here by the commence
ment of work on the east end.


To-day 100 men were put TO work clear
ing the trees and underground from the
right-ot-way. and in less than three weeks
over 1000 will be at work constructing the
bitches and in making ready for the locks.
The men are being taken from the ranks
of the unemployed in this district, and
will be given steady employment.


This canal, with the Chicago drainage
canal and Illinois River, is to form IN i'm
portant waterway connecting the North
western States with the Chicago grain
market, which is now being rushed with
as much vigor as the present and future
appropriations of Congress will allow.


The route at the east end for distance
of thirty-fve miles has been definitely
settled upon. Twelve miles of this dis
lance has been condemned by the United
States District Court and eight miles has
been paid for and possession secured. Ad-
ditional tracks are now being condemned
as fast as the machinery of the court can
operate. Next Monday the contract for
the first four miles will be let, with the
provision that active work be commenced
by the contractors within ten days. The
excavations will then be commenced along
the entire four miles under the supervision
OF twenty Government employees. The
contracts will be let for each mile and each
lock separately.

Death in one of its most awful forms
came last night to a bright little boy whose
home is overshadowed by the palaces OF
Mob Hill. The child was Lynn, the r.
year-old son of Frank Smith, book
keeper who moved into an old house at the
END OF Frank place two or three months
ago. The place is short, narrow street
running westward from Mason, between
California and Pine. The boy was the
eldest of family of seven. bright beyond
his years. and general favorite in the
neigh5orhood.


One OF the seven children was injured
during the day by falling from morse
and the father. after sitting by his side
for several hours, left the house with him
about $3.50 O'Clock in the evening to stroll
around the hill Mrs. Smith was sitting
in the kitchen preparing the younger chill
dren for bed when the lamp that lighted
the little apartment fell to the floor and
exploded. The blazing oil ran over the
carpet and set fire to the chairs. The chill
dren screamed with fright, and Mrs.
Smith, after throwing few pals OF water
on the flames. decided TO leave the house
and call upon the neighbors for assistance


Lynn. the eldest boy. was lying asleep
on the floor Of an adjoining room. and his
mother, thinking that he was not In the
house, gathered the little ones about her
and rushed out of the building, leaving the
kitchen in flames. She fastened TO the
house OF friend in the nelghborhood ana
asked man that she met on the way TO
sound an alarm. The man took his time,
and several minutes had passed belore the
bell on Brenham rlace struck the number.
Meantime crowd nad gathered III the
narrow alley, ana the men who looked into
the burning building saw the child lying
on his back and completely surrounded
Dy flames. His hands were clasped over
his face and he lay still. They made sew
eral efforts to reach him, but were driven
back by the intense heat. which rapidly
burned the body into ciBder. When the
firemen reached the house they. too, tried
TO reach the body, but were driven back
until the room had been drenched with
water. Then the black inanimate form
was taken out and laid upon little bank
of earth, where it remained until the
Cor0neI's wagon came.


The unhappy father and mother soon
learned of the awful fate that had over.
taken their first born. She heard of her
af1liction from neighbor. and rushed
screaming and wallllg back to the build
ing, which Was burning from foundation
to the roof. Kind hands pulled her back
from the spot where the child's body lay,
and led her half fainting TO the dwelling
of a friend or Mason street.


Smith reached the scene before the fire.
men had succeeded IN removing the body
from the house. He was beside himself
with grief and passed the narrow alley
back and forth like one in dream. When
he saw the remains of his child he sobbed
and wept as If his. heart was breaking.
Fearing that his mind would give way If
he were permitted to remain he was in
duced to leave the spot, and subsequently
made his way to the house in which his
wife and children were surrounded by
sympathetic friends. They will remain
there until they are able TO find another
home.


The house, which was owned by Fl. n
Spauldlng, was rendered unfit for habita.
ton by the fire, and the furniture owned
by the stricken family was ruined. Their
loss will amount to about $500. The own
er of the building will lose about $1,000.

The hard times prevailing throughout the
country are less evident at Washington
than elsewhere. The great government mill
runs forever on full time, and the army
of government employees receive several
million dollars from the treasury each
month, all of which goes Immediately into
local circulation. Washington, besides, is a
city where much outside money is brought
to be spent. More great houses are closed
or rented this season than ever before;
more furnished houses were offered for
rent than was ever known to be the case:
and more prominent families have gone to
Europe, gone south, or remained at sum-
mer country homes than can be counted
But new officials, new winter residents,
and season visitors have come, too and
the winter starts with sufficient promise
of social interest and gayety. Political and
International affairs have been almost too
exciting, and the bitterness of legislative
and diplomatic questions has invaded draw
ing rooms to a degree never known before
The very school children talk Hawaii, and
can pronounce Liliuokalani without a stam-
mer. and the boiling kettle is often only
symbolic of the conversation raging around
some tea table.

Queen arrived from silka this afternoon,
anu reported that Capt. HuntleF, the third
mate and fifteen survivors Of the whaling
bark James Alien, wrecked in Western
Alaska, had arrived at Sitka and taken
passage for san Francisco on the steamer
Crescent City. The survivors report that
they endured great hariships and were re-
duced to such circumstances as TO be CON-
PEELED TO eat the flesh OF their dead CON-
rades. Four men were drowned by boat
capsizing and two died of starvation. Eff
teen more are missing.


First Assistant Engineer II. 2. Norton,
Of the United States maa-of-war Concord,
who accompanied Capt. Huntley and the
ship wrecked crew from Unalaska to Sitka,
arrived today and gave the Associated
Press correspondent an account of the dis
aster and the subsequent rescue, as related
to him by the officers and crew. Ten
minutes from the time the whaling bark
Allen struck the reef, she was total
wreck and had gone TO tie bottom. There
was barely time to get into the lifeboats
aud embark. The night was very
dark and stormy, perfect gale
was blowing, and the place where
the accident occurred was six miles from
shore. After the captain got clear Of the
vessel he found himself In the company of
two other boats. They kept together and
weathered the storm until daybreak, when
two boats were found 10 be leaking
badly, and were abandoned, the crew of
twenty men emharking in the other two
boats. In pelting rain and bitter cold
weather, without food, clothing or FIRE,
they beat about among the islands several
days. living on raw shellfish. Subsequently
a storm arose. and while attempting
TO effect landing one boat
capsized and four of the men
were drowned. They landed on Sequin
island. near Attu. Not being able to find
any natives. and suffering greatly from
cold and hunger. Capt HuntIey called for
volunteers to go tosUnalaska for assist
ance. Some difficulty was experienced in
getting the requisite number 10 undertake
the voyage. They left fifteen men, mostly
of foreign birth, on the island. and sailed
eastward. About ten days later they fell
half-famished condition.


After Capt. Huntley departed the crew
became disheartened. One man died from
hunger, and few days later another died
of starvation. The crew alter being res
cued admitted that they had fed off the
flesh OF their dead comrades. The men
were starving, and as soon as one of the
crew began the awful meal the others
quickly followed, and sill ravenously en-
gagged in the fearful feast of human flesh.


Two weeks after Capt. Huntley left the
Bear returned and rescued the men from
their island prison. Some of them had
almost lost their reason. and acted more
like wild animals than human beings.
They were carefully treated and all are
now in fair way TO recover. The revenue
cutter and men-of-war cruised around the
island for two weeks. searching for the
first mates boat and the fifteen men,
This is the number that has not been
accounted for. Capt Huntley has hopes
that they may have landed on some island
or been rescued by some sailing vessel.

PORT TOWNSEND, Wash, August 30
The City Of Topeka. which arrived from
Juneau. gives details of a fierce battle
among the Chilcat Indians, which resulted
in six men being murdered and large
number wounded The Indians were drunk,
and, being armed, did great damage to
themselves. A few days previous to the
fight two Canadian sloops from British CO.
lumbia arrived at Chilcat laden with a vile
quality of liquor. Large quantities were
soon dispensed with in exchange for furs,
etc


Then began a scene of savage orgy. The
Indians are naturally savage and hostile,
and when affected by whisky become wild
demons Immense fires were started, and
several hundred Indians assembled to
drink liquor and dance


Toward morning a dispute arose over a
trivial matter, which resulted in the leader
of one faction being stabbed to death. The
Indians then divided into two parties. and
battle commenced The two whisky
smugglers, unobserved, slipped away from
the scene.


No white people knew the incidents of
the battle. Settlers living few miles dis
tant heard yelling, and, surmising the
origin Of the trouble, dared not venture to
the neighborhood until late in the after
noon of the next day.


I.
wounded Indians were lying all around the
village. Some were frightfully mutilated
and others were suffering agonies from
their treatment. small band of survi-
vors, elated with success and thrsting for
more blood had gone down the beach.
threatening to return and embark a crowd
or savages and annhilate the white set
tiers In the vicinity The white people be-
came alarmed and sent TO Juneau for as
sistance.


Just before the Topeka sailed Deputy
Collector of Customs Slater and a posse
had arrived on the steamer Wrestler and
started for Chilcat to arrest the SNUG
glers. seize the liquor and quiet the In
dians


The Chilcat Indians are hostile tribe.
Only during recent years have they per-
mitted the white traders to enter their
country. Frequently they interfere with
miners crossing the divide into the Yukon
country. On several occasions the gov
ernor has had to send a revenue cutter
there to suppress disturbances.


All this spring on different occasions
unknown white men coming down the coast
in open boats were robbed and murdered.
There are now two or three Indians in the
Sitka Jail charged with murders. The Chill
cats believe in witchcraft and several
women have been put to death in recent
years charged with being witches.

The Jury in the case OF the Maldonado
brothers brought in verdict last night
of guilty.


The Maldonsdos, who are brothers
and both young men, were charged
with attempting to wreck train, on the
Terminal railway during November last.
At the time both men were undoubtedly
drunk, and resenting fsncied insult
from the conductor, attempted to derail
the train by placing tie across the
track, at q point where the line over
hung steep bluff.


The obstruction was seen by passer-
by and removed in the nick OF time.
The came night both OF the youths were
arrested by Detective lnsley.


On the first trial the jury disagreed,
presumably on the score OF the tie hav-
ing been placed on the track by only one
of the defendants. They were retired,
with the above result.


Since the passing OF the statutes
against train wrecking there have been
only three trials for the otfense.


On two OF the occasions the charges
were not proven, and the Msldonados
are the first offenders convicted under
the new law.


The extreme penalty under the statute
under which these defendants were con-
victed is five years imprisonment. The
jury recommended that the full penalty
be given in the present case.


There are two clauses to the statute,
one making life imprisonment or death
the penalty for derailing a train, and
the other fixing the maximum penalty
for putting obstruction on railway
with malicious intent.

To brandy peaches you take large
white or yellow free-stone peaches that
are not too ripe. Scald them with boil
ing water, cover and let stand until the
water becomes cold. Repeat this scald-
ing, then take them out, lay them on a
soft cloth, cover them over with another
cloth and let them remain until perfectly
dry. Now put them in stone jars and
cover with brandy. Tie paper over
the tops OF the Jars and let them re-
main in this way one week. Then
make syrup, allowing one pound of
granulated sugar and half-pint of
water to each pound OF peaches. Boil
and skim the syrup. Then put in the
peaches and simmer until tender. Then
lake the peaches out, drain, and put
them in glass Jars. Stand the syrup
aside to cool. When cold mix equal
quantities OF this syrup and the brandy
In which you had the peaches. Pour
this over the peaches and seal.

The Transvaal police department, which

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal. March 13.-The
United States man-of-war Marion, which
should have been well on her way to this
port, is at Yokohama undergoing extensive
repairs. About fortnight ago cable
gram was received here from Yokohama
saying that the vessel had sailed, but had
been obliged to return for repairs.


The steamer Gaelic, which has arrived
from the orient, brings news that the dam
age was very serious. Two days after the
Marion left Yokohama the vessel encoun-
tered a terrific typhoon in the China So a,
which nearly wrecked her. A long time she
was on her beam ends, and a portion OF
the rigging was carried away and heavy
seas swept over her, cutting the deck
houses aid setting everything on deck
awash. The water poured into the cabins
and down into the engine rooms, and the
boilers were washed from their fastenings.
The fires were extinguished as quickly as
possible, and the man-of-war scudded along
under bare poles before the wind. She rode
safely through the storm and sailed back
to Yokohama.


The full extent OF the repairs TO be made
was not known when the Gaelic sailed, but
II Is estimated that she will be On dock for
at least two months.

Gen. Armstrong, acting commissioner of
Indian affairs. says that the annual reports
received from the various Indian agencies
show that on the whole the Indians were
reasc nably prosperous during the last fiscal
year. The death rate has not been large.
nor does there appear to be any decrease
in the number of Indians under the charge
Of the government. The year was one of
peace. there having been very few dis
turbances or troubles usually occurring
among the Indians. 1t is evident, from the
reports received. that the tribal relations of
the Indians are becoming less binding, and
the individual Indians are becoming more
independent Of tribe and more seif-reliant
The allotting agents of the government
have been kept busy the past year, many of
the Indians evincing desires to own their
own land. The Indian authorities believe
that in allotting tracts of land to individual
Indians the longest step has been made
toward civilization, and that the Indians
are more easily governed by the agents and
the bureau when each has a personal and
Individual interest in his home. The re-
ports show that Indian education is pro-
crossing quite satisfactorily, and that the
Indians show greater willingness than here
tofore to avail themselves of the school adj
vantages offered by the government.

hall over the Old Market last night, the final
night of the grand food exposition. 1t took
at least fifteen inmates tc work ones way
from one end of the hall to the other so dense
was the throng in every aisle.

greater than the night preceding, and the
crowd last night was fitting climax TO the
whole. The universal verdict of all who

most satisfactory and the best that ever vis-

ton, have made themselves solid with the
public.

have engineered the exposition from begin
ming 10 end. deserve credit for conducting
the first really successful food exposition ever
held in Washington, and many and loud were
the congratulations showered upon them last
evening by host of admiring friends.

PORTLAND. Or, July 6.-The longshore-

grievance, but went out in obedience to
an order received from General Master
Workman Sovereign. Steamer officials

non-union men. who are now unloading
the steamer without any interference on
the part of the strikers.


At 5 o'clock this afternoon a crowd of
about 800 men gathered at the union depot
and tried to persuade the engineer and
fireman on the Southern Pacific McMinn-
Vile express to desert their posts. They
refused and took the train out. The
crowd then retired from the terminal
grounds and waited until the California
express would be ready to go out at 6:15.
A few minutes before the train was ready
to start they reformed and marched to
the depot again. A few yards from the
engine they were stopped by squad of
police and Deputy Marshals. While they
were parleying, the time for the departure
of the train arrived and the engineer
pulled out. passing through the crowd. AS
the train passed them they contented

Another innovation has made its APP
pearance at the capitol. 1t is worth

The room in which the supreme court
justices adorn themselves with their
flowing silk robes is across the hall
from the chamber in which the court
meets. Hitherto fow moments before
noon the door of the attiring room
would open, and forthwith would
emerge the solemn justices. On one
side of the corridor-which, by the
way, is the main passageway through
the capitol-would stand a court Off
cial and another man would be sta
toned on the opposite side. Between
this guard the justices would walk and
moment later would disappear behind
the heavy door of the entrance to the
private corridor to the bench. But this
simple and modest method has been
relegated to the past. 1t is different
now.


When the justices are now ready to
leave their attiring apartment, four
court messengers appear. They bear
two pieces of plush covered rope. A
man stands On each side of the two
doors, and across the corridor they
stretch their plush covered barrier.
Through the avenue thus formed the
black gowned justices walk, the bril-
liant plush covering cleaning like
streak of fire against their somber robes.


If the justices are little slow, the
crowd must possess its soul in patience.
Not until the last black gown has dis
appeared are the plush covered ropes
taken down and the ordinary course of
travel allowed to resume. Washing

From Life.


The disputes preliminary to the playing
of the university foot ball have been con-
Quoted this year with customary vigor.
especially the dispute between Yale and
Princeton. There are good points about
these preliminary disputes as compared
with the game itself. Nobody gets hurt in
the disputes, whereas in the games there
are sometimes casualties. Moreover, the
disputes always last a long time, and are
earnest and we'll contested, whereas the
games are brief at best and sometimes
one sided. The disputes, too, are easier and
cheaper to attend than the games. The
newspapers always have reports about
them which one may read to repletion at
small expense and only moderate inconven-
ience. There seems, therefore, TO be much
to favor the conclusion that to have
lively preliminary dispute and no game is
an ideal condition. If the Yale-Princeton
difference should come to that issue this
year the people will have had a rare intel
lectual treat, and the traditional superior
ity OF mind over matter will have been
demonstrated anew.

Not long ago a young lady was lying
half awake in bed in an old house in Bos-
toms suburbs. Suddenly she became who'll
ly awake with the consciousness that a
mouse was running over her chest She
had presence of mind enough not to move,
reasoning that the mouse would presently
run away without harming her. But in
stead of running away the little creature
crept into her neck. and there nestled COM
fortably down, his back curled against the
lower part of her cheek, which lay on the
pillow. The ladys blood was simply frozen
with horror. but she did not dare to move
fearing that the mouse would bite her IL
she did. Collecting her wits, she finally re-
solved that she would, by mighty and
sudden effort, jump sdewise in the bed
away from the mouse leaving him high and
dry on the pillow, and then get quickly up
and out Of the bed on the other side She
would count three and then jump. She
counted one, two, thrse-and then she did
not jump. The mouse nestled comfortably
closer to her neck. She began again and
counted one, two, threei This time she
Jumped sidewise, downward upward and
every way, and screamed besides at the top
OF her voice. What ever became of the
mouse could not be learned, for when all
the family came. with lamps and pokers
and various other weapons, to her aid. no
trace Of the poor little creature could be
found Perhaps he was frightened entirely
out OF existence by the young Iady's
screams.

ATLANTIC HIGHLANDS, N. j., Sept.

structure with nearly 200 rooms, was
completely destroyed by fire early this
morning. There were no guests in the
building at the time, the hotel having
closed for the season few weeks ago.
Watchmen John Rise and Hugh Nc
Connell, with the latter's wife and child,
were in charge of the place They had
a narrow escape from death, and were
compelled to leave the hotel In their
night dresses. A big Newfoundland dog
belonging to Rise perished in the flames


The total loss is estimated at nearly
500 900. The hotel was insured for $45,-
900 in various companies in New York.
: and the furniture for 800. The build
ing was erected eleven years ago. and
was owned by Obermeir & Morton, who
were In an adjoining cottage when the
fire broke out.


1t was nearly o'clock when the
flames were discovered, and residents
of the town were awakened by the
Changing of the alarm bell Hen Addi-
son, conductor of the Barnegat train,
jumped upon a locomotive and directed


e engineer to open up his whistle.
several other iron horses Joined in the
chorus, until not only the whole town
was awakened, but Hillside, Navesink,

Monmouth and Chapel Hill were ex-
cited.


THE several truck and hose companies
we're early on the scene, and powerful
streams were thrown upon the build
ing, but with little effect, for the fire
burned rapidly, and in two hours only
heap of blackened ashes marked the
spot where the handsome structure once
stood.


In escaping from the burning building
0'Connells child became bewlldered in
the smoke and ran towards the locked
entrance to the corridor. She was res
cued with great difficulty.


The scene was most dramatic. Thou
sands of men, women and children gath
cred in Bay View and adjoining ave-
nues and upon the lawns of the nearby
cottages. The 'firemen did good work
plentiful. but not adequate to extin-
Mrs. e. H: Hooper, of the Windsor
Hotel, supplied the nearly exhausted
firemen with hot coffee.


Tne hotel site was the best, over

the scene of a banquet upon the occa-
sion of the opening of the Central and

There are few things more disagreeable
than to put on pair of stiff. brittle shoes
that have been thrown aside to dry
after a rainy day. Here is formula
that claims to eradicate the trouble:
First wipe off gently with soft cloth
all surface water and mud; then, while
still wet. rub well with paraffine oil, using
flannel for the purpose. Set them aside
till partially dry. when a second treat
ment with oil is advisable. They may
then be deposited in a conveniently
warm place. where they will dry gradu-
ally and thoroughly. Before applying
French kid dressing, give them n final
rubbing with the flannel. still slightly
darpened with paraftine and the boots
will be soft and flexible as new kid
and be very little affected by their bath
in the rain.

ASTORIA. Or. Nov. 19.-Tle British
bark Swanmore, 1871 tons, in ballast.
twenty-one days from San Francisco, ar
rived at 80 o'clock this afternoon. Cap
tain Greenbaum has an interesting story
10 ell of the narrow escape of his vessel
from going ashore near Cape Falcon. or
False Tillamook. early yesterday morning.


The Swanmore arrived off the lightship
about O'Clock Saturday afternoon, and
finding no tug or pilot stood off to the
southwark, wind having sprung up from
the northeast. Early Sunday morning the
wind died way and the Swanmore found
herself enveloped in thick fog, and be-
ing unable 20 locate their bearings the
navigstors were completely lost until they
were startled to hear a noise that always
causes the sailors blood to run cold-the
roaring OF the breakers on the beach. The
anchor was at once dropped and thirty
five fathoms of chain run out. here they
remained until $50 o'clock when light
off-shore wind sprung up and the bark's
anchor was slipped. They stood directly
off shore for eight miles and the wind
again failed them. Again the vessel
dr.fted toward the breakers, and their
dull, roaring sound was plainly audible,





Swanmore was headed for the open sea.


By this time the fog had lifted and the
crew of the Swanmore could easily dis
tinguish the rugged and perpendicular
cliff of Cape Falcon. AT o'clock they
were nearly eight miles off shore. when
they were again becaImsd and drifted
shoreward. Nearer and nearer the ireach-
erous land swell carried them, until the
H. hy.a
directly off the worst part of the rugged
headland. She was drifting SLOWLY ashore
and the boats were already filled with the
effects of the crew. ready the moment the
vessel struck TO clear away and attempt
to get to shore through the surf.


Assistance was at hand, however, for
the little steam coaster Harrison doomed
up to the south. The crew of the steamer
had evidently noticed the Swanmore's sig
nails of distress, for they were bearing
down on her under full head Of steam.
The Swanmore was inside the second line
of tumbling breakers and dangerously near
the third when the Harrison managed to
get hold of steel bawser from the vessel.
By this time the roar of the breakers was
deafening and the swell was running
shorewards with terrible force, and when
the line was pulled taut and the little
steamer started with her heavy tow her
bits were nearly torn from her deck.


1t was long and hard struggle at first,
but the Harrison fin llv got the bark free
frcm the breakers. and towing her fully
ten miles off shore dropped her. This
morning she was opposite the mouth of
the river and was picked up by tug and
brought inside. CAPTAIN Schrader of the
Harrison claims that no bargain was
made; in fact there was no time for
striking bargains. On the other hand.
Captain Green baum of the Swanmore
claims that bargain was made for the
sum of 5000.

In Canada perhaps ten thousand women

nasiums of the fashionable boarding schools

pants are worn by the fashionable set for

men. The bathing dress shows marked
signs of following the general movement,

when the ladies left the water there was no
tight-sticking skirt to interfere with their loco

ceDting the trousers. There is the one-button

is no wonder people are talking OF the women

CHICAGO, July 1.-Two deputy United
States marshals met their deaths and two
others were more or less injured this after
noon in a collision OF freight trains on the
Wisconsin Central tracks near the Six
teenth and Jackson streets crossing. The
locomotives and several cars were wrecked
in the accident, and the three-story
brick warehouse of Smith, Burdette & Co.,
was partially destroyed. The dead are:
J. b. Bristol, deputy United States mar
shal; w. A. Pross. deputy United States
marshal. The injured are: Andrew
Blaas. deputy United States marshal. left
foot and leg mangled, condition critical;
Augustine Wright, deputy United States
marshal from Baltimore, not serious.


The Baltimore & Ohio and Wisconsin
Central jointly use this track, and by some
misunderstanding of orders, the trains
were moving towards each other on the
same track. The two engines came to-
gether with a tremendous impact. Fire
broke out in the wreckage, but was soon
controlled. The train crews saved them
selves by jumping.

PORT TOWNSEND, Wash. Dec. 12.-The
steamer Bertha. from Unalaska, brought
the British ship Scot Dales of Liver
pool. Captain Timothy Mccarthy. into
port Tonight partly dismantled. The ship
was bound from San francisco TO Port
land 10 load wheat for Europe.


She left the former port December 2.
and three days later, ahead of moderate
gales, reached the Columbia River.
Thursday and Friday the gale increased to
a hurricane. which created a heavy sea.
Saturday the gale was composed of a sue
cession of bursting squalls, which tore her
sails into tatters and brought down the
foretopmast and all the tore yards and
main upper yards.


The crew became frightened and wanted
to abandon the vessel and take to the
boats. Saturday night the gale continued
with unabated fury and the ship, Iaboring
heavily. strained her hull. Sunday morn
ing the gale subsidized and calm ensued.
leaving the ship rolling in fearful seas.
Suddenly her ballast shifted to the star
board side, badly injuring three men. The
port anchor and thirty fathoms of chain
were dropped overheard as drag to keep
the vessels head TO the sea. Later the
anchor and chain were lost and she went
over on her beam ends. mountainous seas
sweeping her decks, and the only way the
crew could handle the vessel was to lash
themselves to stationary objects. By
trimming the ballast she righted some
what, and then the storm came on again.
carrying away more of the rigging.


The officers and crew mutinied. They
refused to obey their captains commands
and attempted to leave the ship in the
boats. Captain Mccarthy armed himself
and. single-handed. prevented them from
leaving the ship. On several occasions
the vessel was close ashore and In immi-
nent danger of drifting on the rocks,
Twice she got inside the ightship at the
Columbia River bar, when snow began
falling and the increasing gale drove her
out to sea.


Yesterday morning she headed toward
the Straits of Juan de Fuca, but was un-
able to make the cape. In trying to launch
boat one man was dashed against the
side of the ship and killed. Drifting past
Flattery. the ship was slowly going toward
the Vancouver shore, when the steamer
Bertha hove in sight and took her in tow
at o'clock last night.


The Scottish Dales presents dilapidated
appearance. The damage. excepting a
claim for salvage by the Bertha, amounts
to $4,000.


Captain Mccarthy, who has been to sea
over thirty years. says the storm was the
severest he ever experienced.

Most Of the Common wealers stranded here

erty. telling them that a train was being
made up, and any man attempting to
board the train would be shot. The entire

pathzng with the Common wealers. A
pnblc meeting was called and Mayor
Douglass elected chairman. Speeches

committee of eight was elected to confer
with officials ana the Industrials. Super
intendent Calvin and Pinkham were will
ing to do all they could for the relief OF
the citizens, but their hands we're tied by
the court. The Industrials were deter
mined to ride East. The men were again
ordered to get off the train, but refused.
Dick Williams, constable OF the town,
made himself conspicuous encouraging the
Industrials, and was arrested and taken to
Jail No key was found. and he was
handcuffed and taken to Calvin's car.
The Industrials threatened to release him.
and crowded around the car confronted by

out commander. The train was pulled

ST. PAUL, May 1.-After being tied up

ern system will now resume work. the
great strike being declared off tonight.

can Railway Union and President Debs,
although the commercial bodies of the two
cities were largely responsible for the
result.


Various conferences were held by the
committees with President Hill and with

nounced in favor of arbitration all along.

the men would resume work.

this afternoon. and the result is the strike
has been declared. off and the men will re-
turn to work at once. The conference
went over all details thoroughly, and MIR.
Hill made concessions 10 the men. the re-
suit being that the whole diffic lty was
settled then and there.


1t was settled really by arbitration, the
citizens committee being the judges, but
the strikers gained all their demands,
while the company secured a settlement
through ar bitration as Hill desired.


The 1900 miles of track will be open ed
for business by over 5000 employees and the
entire Northwest will be released from the
freight and passenger blockade that has
oppressed It for over two weeks.

throwing herself from fourt history

She plunged out head first and struck

She was dead when her eldest son. Ed
ward, reached her a few moments later.


Mrs. Burbach's husband died in Ger
many nine years ago. With her three
sons she came to America six years ago.
Edward, then twenty-one years old, Sc
cured work at his trade of stone-cut-
| ting.


Edward Is married. and is the main
support of the home where his mother
met her violent death this morning.
For nearly a year Mrs. Burbach had
been an invalid, suffering from heart
disease and asthma. Last Wednesday
she developed symptoms of insanity.
Since then the younger members Of the
family kept a watch over the sufferers
movements, remaining by her bedside
day and night.


During the day Edwards wife would
remain in attendance. and at night the
sons would administer whatever COM
fort they could to their helpless mother.


Their physician called late last night.
His patient was then more or less vio-
lent. She got out OF bed several times
and insisted on sitting up.


Edward remained with her until $50
this morning, when she seemed compare
lively quiet Tired out with watching he
kissed her and lay down on his bed in
the adjoining room.


Ten minutes later Edward jumped
from his bed. He had dreamed that a
policeman was carrying his mother
away. He rushed into the bedroom, and
found that she was gone. Running into
the kitchen, he was just in time to see
his mother dive headlong through an
open window.

SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 21.-Mrs. Sophia
Beresford. wife of a prosperous drayman,
died last night of CHAMBERS. Four weeks
ago the woman's husband unwittingly pur-
chased diseased horse for the family to
drive. A few days later. while Mrs. Beres-
ford was standing near the horses head the
animal sneezed in her face. Soon after
ward she was stricken with chills and
pains and swelling of the forehead. She
finally became SO bad that she was re-
moved to the hospital. and there the true
nature of the disease was discovered-the
whole upper portion of the woman's face
was eaten away by the dread disease. The
husband and children have also been ex-
posed, and their condition is being closely
watched The health authorities killed the
horse. and will cause the arrest of the
traders who sold 1t to Beresford at a price
which was ridiculously low.

Judge Knapp Of the interstate commerce
commission was before the Senate committee
on interstate commerce yesterday and made a
statement bearing upon the bill for the regu-
lation of railroad pooling advancing the idea
that railroads could afford to move freight at
an average charge of 80 cents per mile for the
car. Attorney Cowen OF the Baltimore and
OHIO, and Attorney Bond ofthe Richmond and
Danviile, who were present, took exception to
this statement saying that the estimate must
be for running expenses only and that it did
not take into account the original investment.
the interest account, the vexatious DELAYS
which often occur nor the fact that many cars
are often idle. Mr.. Knapp admitted that he
had estimated for running expenses only.

The Weather Bureau in its weekly snow
chart issue says: North Dakota and portions
of Minnesota are now covered with nearly a
foot of snow, and over portions OF the upper
Michigan peninsula more than foot and a
half is reported. While the southern limit of
area covered extends southwark into Ohio
and western Pennsylvania. there is but little
snow on the ground eastward of lower Michi-
gan, the greatest depth over the region
named being three inches at Pittsburg. The
last decade of March, 1894. has been charac-
terized by the most remarkable temperature.
extremes occurring in March that have been
recorded since the establishment of the
Weather Bureau. Within six days. over a
large portion of the country. east of the
Rocky mountains, both the highest and low
est temperatures yet observed during March
have been reported.

The house was a fve-story brick tepe-

The adaptability of rats and cats to all
diversities of climate is exemplified by their
presence and activity in the coid-storage

nue. warehouses were unable 10 stand the
exposure and died. However an unusually
hardy colony stuck to Il, and their progeny
are now provided with wonderfully long
and thick hair, even their long tails being
covered with fur. They have developed into
fat old rascals. and the cats which were
introduced to thin their ranks have also

bounty The cats have developed very close,
thick fur, and their whiskers have grown

A small black cat with a long tail and
a distinctively aggrieved air stalked up
and down the hall at Herman's Howard
Auditorium in Baltimore. She glared
with scorn at the people who came out
of the maze and laughed as II they
thought 1t was funny in there. The cat
had been In there, too, but she didn't
think 1t at all funny, says an exchange.


II she had been a cat with human Vices
she might have believed her experience
was due to drink but as she took nothing
stronger than milk she couldn't fall back
on that explanation.


The cat went into the maze for the
first time although her curiosity had
sorely tempted her to enter ever since
the maze had been put into position. She
strolled in and climbed pillar near the
door. 1t so happened that this was
central position, and when she threw
her eyes around there seemed to be six
teen other black cats returning her glance
with friendly interest. This enraged her,
and she bumped her back to let the other
cats know she was no coward Sixteen
other cats took a corresponding hump,
and each was watching her next move.


This was too much, and the cat leaped
from her stand and started to get out.
There were apparently a dozen avenues
Of escape, and she made for one of them,
only to run plump against glass mirror.
The same thing happened again and
again until she finally sped the man In
blue uniform who takes tickets for the
maze. Like a flash she leaped past him
and got ont of the maze.

ment declare that the veto Of the Bland bill
shows that the administration has set its face
toward the single gold standard.


Representative McLaurin Dem }. Of South
Carolina, has taken the bold initiative In this
step. He has prepared the proposition, and
1t will be followed, he says, by a call signed
by Democratic silver Congressman. Con-
cerning the movement he authorizes the fol-
lowing statement:


SIT seems to me that the condition of our
country is such that it should impel true men
to ri Sc above partisan and factional consider
ations.


1.-The veto OF the seigniorage bill by Presi-
dent Cleveland forces distinct issue between
the South and the West and the East and
the North. The South and the West are the
borrowing and producing sections, while the
North and the East are the loaning and con-
suming sections. The South and the West
demand higher prices for their products,
which is but another name for cheaper
money. The North and East are striving for
cheaper products, which in turn Is simply
another name for dearer money.


.In this manner the two general divisions of
the country are arrayed against each other.
The North and East have for many years con-
trolled all legislation, and as natural result
have enacted laws favorable to their own Sec
ton and against the South and West


"The money of the country has been gradu-
ally and almost surreptitiously taken from
the people, and as a necessary sequence the
prices Of all products have declined.


''This manipulation Of the currency has
continued until every product OF the
South and West are to-day sold for less
than the cost of production. The resultant
effect OF these abnormally low prices is seen
in the rapid accumulation Of debts and the in
creasing distress among the people.


81 believe the time has come when the
South and West should unite in one mighty
effort for self-protection- 1 want to see the
cotton planter of my own section and the
wheat producer of the West unite and make
a contest for higher prices and happier condi-
tions."

Mrs. Hettie Russell, of No 50 81 street north
east, is greatly distressed because, she says,
her thirteen-year- old boy Charlie has been taken
from her and she Is unable TO ascertain what
has become of him.


Mrs. Russell last night told TINES reporter
pitifuI story, which shows that she has had
more trouble than generally falls to the lot Of
one woman, and the recital of which will no
doubt awaken sympathy in many a heart


Mrs Russell was left widow seven years ago,
her husband dying after long illness She had
i've children to care for-the eldest, girl Of
twelve, and the youngest,a girl of two. Tho
latter was afflicted with congestion Of the brain,
which was followed with blindness, and the
mother was compelled to work for her living
and was unable to properly care for her baby
Mrs Russell was compelled to part with the
little one and send her to the Asylum for the
Blind at Baltimore.


The other children were in comparatively good
health, and Mrs. Russell kept them with her for
time, although 1t was desperate struggle for
her to provide food and clothing for them all.
She did not murmur, however, and it was not
until about four years ago that, finding that dur
ing her absence from home at work Charlie, the
youngest boy and Mary, the second daughter,
were not being properly taken care Of she
sought and obtained permission for them TO
enter the Washington Orphan Asylum, corner of
Fourteenth and streets northwest, as inmates.
/ Mrs. Russell visited her children frequently
as the rules of the institution permitted, and
she was measurably happily in the fact that she
could see her loved ones frequently, though she
was not able to care for them personally.


HER BOY HAD DISAPPEARED.


She was dumbfounded when, making one Of
her usual visits nearly two years ago, she was
told upon inquiry for Charlie that he was away
visiting and would soon return. Mrs. Russell
was told the same thing many times afterward,
and she would have continued to think that the
absence OF her child ON the occasion of her visits
was only sing ular circumstance had not one OF
the little tots who had learned Mrs. Russells
name by seeing her so frequently, said, Mrs. Rus
sell, know where your Charlie has gone. a lady
took him away q long time ago and never
brought him back,


Mrs Russell was Mortified at the information
and begged the matron TO tell her if what the
child had said was true. The matron at first de-
clined 10 give any information on the subject,
bur after much persuasion the part OF the
distressed mother, told the mother that Charlie
mad been adopted by family who would take
good care of him.


For a long period this was the extent of the
information that Mrs Russell could get about
her boy, but some time later the matron yielded
sufficiently to tell Mrs Russell Charlie was with
the family of Alberta Berry, wealthy lady liv-
ing opposite Lower Cedar Point, Md, and that
he was doing well, being loved by his foster par
euts ana lovihg them in return, but whether
they lived in Maryland or Virginia could not be
ascertained.


1t was a great satisfaction 10 Mrs Russell 10
hear this much, but she yearned for letter
from her boy, and she wrote To him telling him
that although her poverty had compelled the
separation between them, she stiu loved him
only mother can.


ALL TRACE LOST.


Long and snxiously the poor mother waited
for reply, but none came from Charlie, and
when a letter did arrive from the post-onlce at
Lower Cedar Point, it was simply the cold, for
NAL official notice accompanying the undeliv-
cred letter that no such person as Mrs. Alberta
time TO the present Mrs Russell has been IN
able TO learn a single syllable concerning her
Lhild.


But there was more trouble in store for her
For many months her oldest boy was unable 10
find employment. until few weeks ago when
On the first day his right hand was caught in the
stamping machine he was running and the end
Of one of his fingers was so badly mashed that
portion OF the finger had to be amputated


Mrs. Russell has been employed for some time
past in running sewing machine in the bindery
at the Government Printing once, but since
Public Printer Benedict took charge Mrs, Rus
sell, with other employees OF that department,
has had little work that il is about all she can
do 10 earn enough to pay rent and keep body
and soul together. few days ago she was
compelled to take a vacation and wait for
her pay until the Goth of next month. She ex-
pressed desire to continue at work, hoping if

She did not desire to give any information rela-

The name OF American. girl was once pop
ular synonym for ''nerves," ill-health and all
the ailments engendered by want of exercise,
foolish diet and irregular habits of life. When
contrasted with the English girl, whose out
door life made her the picture of abounding
health and rosy-cheeked energy, she suffered
in the comparison. A generation has SUI
feed to effect complete change, and our
English cousins no longer hold a monopoly
of outdoor sports. Where thirty years ago
the girl who went boating and fishing. climb
ing trees and jumping fences with her bro
theirs was looked upon as tomboy and re-
garded with severe disapproval, the reverse
is now the case.


Outdoor life. delight in action, the spirit Of
sport, have taken hold of American woman
hood Girls of strong, active physique. erect
carriage and energetic spirit, delighting in
tennis, riding, boating, walking, are now the
rule; the feeble indoor do-nothing is the eX-
ception, and the result is tall. vigorous race,
with free step and cheeks aglow with the
ruddy color of physical health and energy.
Walk along the avenues OF any large city at
the fashionable hours and the procession of
bright. animated girlhood which passes be-
fore ones eyes gives ample proof of summer
activity. All over the country, where there
are men AMI money 10 start club and create
sporting interest. the women also have their
share of advantages, and in not few cases
their fair share also of the work in set
ting the organizations on foot. There are few
country clubs, hunt clubs, tennis clubs, or
other sporting clubs throughout the Union
which have not a lady membership.

Good old times were revived at River View

draw a great crowd to this popular resort.
Extra trips were made by the boats, thus en-
abling the company to handle the crowds
without difficulty.

The great canvas balloon lay all day shape
less mass upon the ground. trench mad

air pipe continued to pour It's contents into
the bag until the whole affair stood taut and
rigid. 1t had been advertised that Miss Ruby

speeches, for yesterday second copy OF them
reached the editorial rooms. The internal
beauties OF Lemuels phamplet are many, but
none OF their burning, soul-thrilling phrases
can equal the one quoted as the caption of
this eulogy, and which appears as motto
on the title page.


None but that wonderful, seething brain Of
Lemuel's could have evolved such ponder
ous truism. To ordinary minds trusts are
combinations of industries to control prices
and plunder the public, but Lemuel, the pro-
found, philosophic Lemuel, has discovered
that to smash industries will protect trusts
and the work OF tariff reform has been in
vain.


Shades Of Washington, Jefferson, and Jack
son. why could not have Lemuel lived sooner,
longer, and more often2 With his deep,
intense, penetrating genius the Constitution
could have been improved, Congress would
have become useless body, and Lemuel,
learned Lemuel, could have been President,
the people, and a little red wagon combined.
But then there Is yet future for Lemuel.
Not for his cool, enhancing speeches, his
unique motto concerning trusts. his re-
markable beauty, nor for anything Lemuel
has done, but where thereis such undeveloped,
transcendant genius something must be the
result.


This future will come to Lemuel Just as his
motto did-a magnificent, crushing idea that
was too long, too prodigious for his brain,
and in an enthusiastic moment it rushed forth

scare among farmers and stock men. All
along the Union Pacific, B. & NJ, Elk Horn,
and various other lines radiating from this
point throughout the State come the tidings

half crop.

different aspect from that of forty-eight hours
since. Many fields that were not expected to
rally under any quantity Of rain under the last
two days downpour are now in normal con-
dition. The crop may average two thirds.

A man-eater shark caught off Hawthorne

was made by Oscar and John Matthews. The two
went out attend to nets which they had
stretched in the Sound and found the big fish
caught in the meshes of the net by the head He
was trying 10 get away and was pulling and tug
cling on the net The boat brought near the
shark and after the monster had exhausted him
self with his struggles long knife fastened 10 an
oar was thrust into his side back Of the left fin.
The shark became frantic and almost upset the
boat In his struggles. The fishermen hauled Off
and waited until. exhausted with his struggles.
the shark lay quietly in the water. The boat was
rowed close the side OF the shark and this time
the knife jabbed twice into his side before
the boat obliged 10 pull out OF the reach OF
the thrashing tail


The fishermen then rowed about to their other
nets and found them in good order. They returned
to the shark in about an hour He was still alive,
but weak and after puncruring him again.
they fastened rope about his tail. Before This
was accomplished he deid. The fishermen
towed their prize to Lyons Rock. where the body
was beached. 1t is thought the shark was tempted
into shoal waters by hunger. He is the largest
caught near Port Chester.

text:
Does Not Change in Life.


From the Louisville Courier Journal


There Is born with every one Of US and
continues unchanged during our lives an
lnfailing and ineradicable mark or marks
which absolutely distinguish each one Of
US from every other fellow-being. These
physical marks never change from the
cradle to the grave. This born autograph
Is impossible to counterfeit and there is no
duplicate Of 1t among the teeming pillows
In the world. Look at the insides Of your
hands and the soles Of your feet, closely
examine the ends Of your fingers; you see
circles and curves and arches and whorls
some prominent with deep corrugations
others minute and delicate. but all well
defined and closely traced pattern. There
is your physiological signature.


Run your hands through your hair and
press your finger nails on a piece Of clear
glass. You see all the delicate tracing
transferred-not two fingers alike even
1.-The left hand knoweth not what the right
hand doeth;" they are all distinctly differ
ent Even twins may be so similar in size
features and general physical conditions
as to be scarcely distinguishable, yet their
finger autographs are radically different


In fact in all humanity every being car
ries with him his baby fingers and his
wrinkled hands Of decrepid old age, the
identical curves. arches and circles that
were born with him. Nothing except dis
memberment can obliterate or disguise
them. Criminals may burn and scar their
hands, but nature, when she restores the
cuticle, invariably brings back the natal
autograph.

foreign country having a representative in

AS the chanting began, the candles were
lighted, lending weird and picturesque
aspect 20 the scene. The Bishop was robed
in elaborate vestments of mis- Office, his
tiara being set with mosaics, rubies and
emeralds woven into jeweled embrolderies,
and his red velvet suTplce being wound

gold and small jewels. The Greek monk
was robed in a lengthy flowing black
gown falling from the top of high head

shaggy bearded face of typical Cossack
of romance. The Bishop and his attend
ants chanted the service alternately; the
acolytes swinging the censor until the air

lasted half an hour, the candles being ex-

Strangers helped in the rescue from

baby. To add to her terror smoke pulled

shouted to Goldstein to hand his wife

window sill and lowered her down until

across the shaft. One false move and all
hands would have fallen into the shaft
and met instant death. The rescuers
were cool, however, and they lifted the
woman over the top of the fence and
finally to the roof. The baby was carried
out moment later. New York Tribune.

Department has received a dispatch from

fleet in the Gulf of Pechili to the ef-

last and inflicted heavy loss.


Japanese feet consisting of nine war
ships and two fast transports, armed and
converted into cruisers, had been sent in
search of the enemy's feet, which was
sighted at noon on Monday thirty miles
east of the island of Hal Yung Pao.


The japanese pursued the enemy at
full speed. The Chinese showed no dispo-
sitiOn to alter their course or to give bat
tie. The chase lasted little over an
hour, the japanese gaining.


Shortly after l o'clock the cruiser Chi
Yota got within range of the Chinese flag
ship. the guns opened fire on her and a
running fight ensued. Several ships on
both sides were quickly engaged. This
lasted for two hours.


The Chinese transports entered the Yalu
River safely during the main engagement
which was fought in the estuary and which
lasted until nightfsll. Three Chinese war
ships were success sfully disabled and sunk,
and one was set on fire and DESTROYED,
Several other of the enemy's warships
were seriously damaged by the heavy fire.


The Japanese warships were so well
handled that not one was lost. Only two
were damaged to any great extent, but
one of the armed transports was badly
crippled and put out of action.


The admiral does not mention the num-
Der of killed or wounded.

which drove the Sterling back and forced

through the teeth of the gale and turned
eastward, taking the course straight across
the South Atlantic. doubling the Cape Of
Good Hope, passing between Tasmania
and New Zealand, and coming thence
across the Pacific to San Diego. The i'm
mense distance was covered in 1873 days.

perb circular porched entrance and

From the south colonnade to the

All of the main buildings. of
the Worlds Fair except the Hortl-
cultural building. the Women's building,

the United States Government building

ministration building. In twenty minutes

with terrible roar and sparks and blaz-
ing brands were carried by the wind north
and northeast to the Mining, Electricity
and Agricultural buildings. The Elec-
tricity building was the first TO take fire.


In few minutes it was enveloped in
flames. and at 7:10 o'clock the glass roof

WOODLAND, April ia special to the
Mail from Winters says that the town is
up in arms over the Chinese question and
streets, making threats against the Chi
nese and Japanese laborers who have
taken the places OF white men.


This is large fruit-growing section and
the ranchers and orchardists have lately
employed large numbers of Chinese and
Japanese, who work for cheaper wages
than the whites. The citizens of Winters
have for some time been 6iscon ented over
the parliality of the ranchers for oriental
labor and Thursday their resentment
broke out in violent manner.


On that day white man named M. G.
Ferry arrived from San Francisco as the
agent of Wah Hing, a Chinese doctor.
Ferry bustled about town drumming up
business for his employer and this was
more than the people of Winters could
stand. Their pent up resentment against
the Orientals broke out. Ferry was
pelted with rotten eggs and otherwise
roughly handled. That night be got out
Of town glad TO be alive.


After paying their respects to Ferry the
townspeOple hung Japanese and Chinese
in effigy. The figures swung in the wind
all night and to-day were burned by the
crowd. A Japanese was caught on the
bridge and after being pounded was
thrown overheard and was quite badly
hurt


To-day the citizens held a meeting and
appointed committee to notify the
ranchers that they must discharge their
Chinese and Japanese laborers.


The feeling against the Grientals is not
onfned to the white laborers alone, for
all the citizens of Winters regard the
rapid increase of the Asialic population as
a bad thing for the town.


The ranchers. however. show no dispo-
sition to give up their cheap labor. and
declare they will continue to employ Chi
nese and Japanese. The people of VIM
ters are equally determined that they
shall not, and unless one side weakens
very soon serious trouble is liable to
occur The Chinese and Japanese are
greatly alarmed and are keeping closely to
their quarters.

The Small Scale on Which One Family


Manages TO Enjoy Life.


The back yard. after the fashion Of city
yards, was not very big, but it was exquisitely
neat. There was a small grass plot some
what larger than table-cloth, on which the
turf was velvety, owing to the tender care Of
the father of the family. The fence was
whitewashed until it was dazzling, and then
its overpowering luster was screened by green
vines. There was a narrow border OF
geraniums and helliotropes next to the fence.
and they blossomed with most amazing bril-
liarcy. The path was guitless of single
weed between its bricks, and even on washing
day the atmosphere OF the yard was one of
great neatness. And last and best, there was
a single rear tree.


There were children in the family. too, but
they were rather proud Of their estate, and
instead Of treading the grass down they took
pleasure in keeping out the weeds and in
raking their diminutive garden patches. They
had their rewards on clear spring Sundays,
when there was always a family garden
party.


On Sundays the table was brought out and
placed beneath the pear tree for luncheon. 1t
was spread with especial daintiness. The
little garden yielded up its choicest blooms
for the cenrre-piece. The salad the cold
meat. the thin sliced bread, the tea urn. and
the great, heaping fruit dish were all placed
as at "a lively rs possible. Then the family
galuered around and laughed and talked and
ate beneath their pear tree and managed to
persuade themselver that they were really
having beautiful time.

PINE CITY, Mimi. Sept. 4.-Grlndstone

control it. The relief party had hardly
reached the scene, however, when they

Patrick started back along the shore.

padded faster than they had ever done
before, hoping to reach the camp before it
was overwhelmed. While they were still
some distance away they saw the women
rushing into the lake and the camp outfit
going skyward in smoke. Patrick hardly
comprehended these things. however, as

1t passed onward in its work of destruc-
ton through the forest His clothing was
ignited, and for time he was completely
dazed

was all about him and only narrow
pathway through to the water at the edge
OIL the lake, where the bank shelved very
steep all along. offered an avenue of es-
cape. AS he was splashing through the
wafer stray dog fell in behind him and
marched along in mis- company. The two
had an encounter little later with a black
bear that barred their passage and would.
under ordinary circumstances, have ami
Inflated both man and dog. Bruin, who
was squatted in the water, did not even
deign to notice them, but simply moved
aside about six inches so that thew could
pass.


They finally reached place where the
road opened out from the lake and here
met twenty-one people, homesteaders and
their families, who had been fleeing
through the binding smoke ahead of the
flames. All the members of the Marty
threw themselves into the lake and re-
NAMED there until the flames had passed
over. None were seriously injured. but
all were so exhausted as to preclude the
possibility of going farther that night.
They lay on the banks of the lake until
morning. than started back over the road

10 the Prince that the people greeted him

As Mr.. Irving Finch, of Binghamton, was
walking across one Of the two bridges over
Indian River, which connects East with West
Main street, he saw curious combat between
ten-pound pickerel and a aseven-pound black
bass, writes the Philadelphia correspondent
of the New York Sun.


Mr.. Finch happened to glance into the
water and saw therein piokerel, whose size
caused him to stop and admire it, swimming
leisurely along. moment after MIR. Finch
stopped the pickerel turned sharply to the
right and dived. A moment later another
fish, black bass, jumped clear out of the
water and fell back with splash, then poised
with fms and tail quiyering while its dorsal
fin was erect and rigid. Two white marks
just above its tail showed whore the pickerel
had siezed it.


A moment later the pickerel returned to the
waters surface and swan ahead OF the bass
about four feet, apparently not noticing the
bass. AS the pickerel swan the bass darted
forward and depressing its course little
went beneath the pickerel so that the dorsal
fin was drawn across the pickerels belly.


AS every one knows, the end Of the bass
dorsal fin is armed with little spurs. and those
OF this bass cut through the pickerels skin
into the intestines The pickerel struggled a
few moments, then turned on its side and
died.


The bass would then have escaped had not
Archie Bolton, small boy who prides him
self with target pistol OF 22-caliber, stopped
while on his way home from an unsuccessful
hunt to watch the fight The boy took careful
aim and shot the bass through the back, kill
ing it. That of course was violating the game
laws but the local game warden, because of
the peculiar circumstances Of the shooting,
has decided not to push the charge.

DEXTER PARK. L. l., April 6.-When the
marksmen in the great American handicap
pigeon shoot left off last night owingto dark
ness there were eleven men with full scores,
having killed twelve birds each, but as the
contest progressed to-day their numbers were
diminished.


The birds were very trying at first, the
wind was anything but in their favor. and
drivers and right quarterers were the rule.
Many of those who thought they had a cinch
were disappointed by some of the birds, which
flew to the right so swiftly that they made
only "tail bird" hits, and consequently
loser.


As anticipated by the Associated Press,
Capt. Money and I. W. Morley made dead
heat, each killing every bird that flew from
the traps presented to them. The wind fresh
ened considerably during the afternoon, and
a more lively set of birds were sprung from
the traps


From the eighteenth round every person
present thought it was foregone conclusion
that one of the two would win, as they had a
clean score. They did not disappoint their
admirers as at the end of the twenty-fifth
round they tied, with a score of twenty-five
killed. Nobody felt disgruntled and each
cpHteStant Warmly SHOOK tne tieu cOnlesttHlS
by the hands. They then made an arrange
ment to shoot off ten birds each at the same
distance, which was allowed by the handicap,
with the result that Morley missed his first
and second birds, which were right-quarters
and drivers, but he ''grassed" his next eight.
In return, the veteran Money killed the same
amount out of the ten, missing twisting
driver (Which was corker) and towerer.


After this the two gentlemen agreed to
match with the conditions miss and out"
Morley won this by using his second barrel
on the first and one barrel on the second
bird. while the veteran hit his first. a right
quarterer, with the second barrel. but missed
a difficult driver on his next shot, thus losing
the first prize of the big match.


The shoot-off for third place was contested
by Messrs. Simpson, Fulford Kleinz. Jones,
Moore. Walters, and J. L. Smith, with the re-
suit that Simpson. Fulford, and Moore had to
shoot off. Fulford withdrew, and Moore got

on the west coast of Africa. Colonel Ellis
reports that Inspector Taylor of the
frontier police was pursuing the Sofs, vino

Kerrayemma on December 81 and found
the place to be perfect charnel-house.
Scores of slaughtered captives, including
women and children. were strewn- about
the streets; sick and wounded people
were seen on all sides, and the stencil
from putrefying bodies was horrible in the
extreme.


Inspector Taylor once more started in
pursuit Of the Sofs who did the bloody
work and came close upon them on Janu-
ary at Bagwema. The frontier police
found the place strongly protected by
blockades and other defenses. The police.
however. carried the place by storm in a
quarter of an hour, killing 200 Sofs and
wounding seventy-seven others. In addi-
ton the police captured all the guns and
ammunition of the Sofis and rescued 400
slaves, the majority of whom were women
and children. The frontier police only
lost TWO men during the engagement.
Four days previously the Sois. under Chief
Fori, attacked the police garrison at Tonkia
Sibul and were repulsed with loss of
fifty killed and a large number wounded.

high.

followed by very cold wave.

southwest indicated that the wires had been
blown down. No reports from the south
west Of the Arkansas valley were received.

WASHINGTON, June 19-The Weather
Bureau in its report of the weather crop
for the week ending June IS says: The
week ending June Is has been much
warmer than usual from New England
westward over the Lake region, the Ohio
and Mississippi valleys and the Dakotas.
About the normal temperature prevailed
from New York southwark. TWAS cooler
than usual throughout the Rocky Noun
tains and plateau districts and over the
greater portion OF the Pacific Coast States.
More than the usual amount of rain fell In
Texas and over the greater portions of
Kansas, Nebraska, Wisconsin and New
York. Small areas of excessive rains were
Also reported in South Dakota.


The drought previously reported in the
Northwestern States has been broken by
recent rains, but small grain crops have
been permanently injured. Light show
ers occurred in Northern California, Ore
gon and Montana, and the crops on the
Pacific Coast were improved, but sunshine
and dry weather are needed in the flooded
regions of Oregon. Generally. the week
has been especially favorable TO corn

VICTORIA, b. c., July 19.-The seal
ing schooner c. d. Rand has returned
from n sealing cruise which was cut
short by a mutiny of Indian hunters.
The first signs of mutiny appeared off
Sitka on June Is, when the wages were
paid. The Indians then lowered their
canoes ana prepared to desert the ship.
owing to new regulations Indians are
the only available hunters for the
Behring Sea. White men cannot use
spears. Indians demanded S. per canoe
extra. To this the captain agreed, and
the Indians returned to the schooner.


The Indians again mutinied and took
possession of the vessel. The mutineers
numbered twenty-one, while the captain
had only five white men and two faith
full Indians to help him. The Indians
threatened to scuttle the vessel, secur-
ing the skins which were in the hold.
Several times the vessel nearly capszed
owing to their bad management


NAt last the captain and his men got
the drop on the mutineers and drove
them into the hold, where they shut
them up. He then sailed for Sitka,
where he obtained handouts from the
Government officials aud brought the
Indians down in irons.

Representatives of the Coxey army made

Atnougn they did not know Ii, the three

able that they could enter the house today,
