text:
Five young men who left North Beach
last Tuesday morning in the sloop Hattie
to enjoy days fishing at California City
had an experience in the bay which they
will remem ber for a long time to come as
the closest approach to death that a man
need ever care 10 make.


The participants in the adventure were
Steve Balk, an attache of engine 3, living
at 2013 Hyde street; Fred Joy and his
brother Billy, extramen with hook and
ladder company 4. living at 1916 Pacific
avenue, and "Lum" Williams and James
Mccain, who reside near the "beach."


For several days they had been making
preparations for fishing excursion, and
finally hired the sloop hattie. and stocked
her up with good things to eat and drink
to make the trip more pleasant


Among the stores were fve-gallOn keg
of beer. large can of milk, sandwich
and the like. The fishing tackle was
safely slowed away, and ere the anchor
was weighed, to make the voyage seem
more realistic Balk was selected as cap
tain, and he in turn appointed Fred Joy
as his first mate. This others were then
given to understand that they were but
ordinary seamen as long as the party was
a1Oat.





TO cross the bay to the Marin County shore,
little thinking of the dangers which they
would have to pass through before they
returned.


Everything went we'll until the boat was
half way across, when she got caught by
the strong wind and was driven out of her
course so much that il was a toss up
whether she would bump against Angel
Island or run into one of the Olympic
Club arks at Belvedere Cove, or whether
the frall craft would whirl around, head
for the Golden Gate and carry the whole
patty out TO the FarallOnes. The Grew"
looked TO the captain for orders, but
Skipper Balk could only gaze helpessly
about and murmur something concerning
''luffing the helm" Soon after giving this
vague order he admitted that he really did
not know what TO do with a sloOp when
she acted in such strange manner in
gale of wind.


Then each one on board became skipper
on his own hook, and under their joint
management the sloop gave the wind
lively tussle. Sometimes she was headed
Tor SausaltO, and at other times her PROV
pointed toward this city.


1t was we'll on in the afternoon when the
sloop, win its weary occupants, swung
into Richardson's Bay, and then the party
landed and refreshed themselves from the
shlpS stores. AS the wind was blowing
in the direction of San Francisco it was
resolved to attempt 20 make the trip back


All we have got to do" said Captain
Balk. who had now recovered his dignity,
is to hold the sail tight and the wind will
blow us over"


Jhe start was made, and the captains
predictions were fulfilled until the strong
tide that swirls toward the Golden Gate
was reached. Then the little sloop began
TO act Queeriy again. The sail suddenly
Tapped around, and under the impulse Ola
gust OF wind the Hattie began to make for
the GoldenGate to the great cons ternation of
those on board. To make matters worse,
night came on just as the sloop was off
Fort Point. The fishermen were now
really panic-stricken. To be carried out to
sea meant death. Fortunately by another
lucky turn Of the sail the sloop was swung
about and wore along the Marin shore
toward California City, the very place
thes had started for. But before getting
there 1t made another tack.


All through the long night the little
craft drlfted around at the mercy of the
wind and tide. while its occupants shiv-
cred with fear and cold. They had long
ago given up all hope of controlling their
vessel. Their provisions were soaked
through BY the waves that rolled over the
sloop and threatened to swamp her. Now
and then 10 revive thems selves they took a
drink of beer or milk. Toward daylight
the supply OF these liquids gave out and
the prospects were cheerless indeed.


Soon after daylight the Hattie ran ashore
again near California City, but the wave
tossed men no longer had any desire TO
catch fish. They wanted to get home, Oh,
SO badly. but wha: waste of water lay
between them and the San Francisco hills


Having dried their drenched clothing in
the sun. and feeling more cheerful now il
was daylight, they again pushed off.


BY about o'clock they had got over by
Alcatraz, and the sloop was plunging very
badly and shipping water, which those on
board kept balling out with the milkcan
and their bats.


The steamer San Rafael on her As trip
from this city slowed up as she approached
them. and her captain hailed them, asking
if thew wanted to be taken aboard. Cap
tain Balk answered, but his crew said
they would stay by the sloop, especially as
she was now beaded toward home


Two hours afterward the party landed
at the old smelling works wharf, at the
foot of Hyde street, thoroughly worn out,
wet TO the skin and, although fshless.
thankful that they had escaped finding a
grave in the same depths that cover the
remains OF many an inexperienced boat
man who trusted to the treacherous winds
and currents of the bay.

And now for Little Rock! At fifteen min
utes before II o'clock tonight the members OF
the National Fencibles champion drill team
will leave Washington for the Arkansas capi-
tai to compete in the interstate company drill
on July 4.


For two hours last night the team drilled at
Convention hall. This WIS their last practice,
and right hard did they work. In a number
of instances the regulation uniform was dis
carded and the boys marched in their shirt
sleeves, without caps or gloves. small num-
Der OF mothers, sisters, and lady friends were
present and thoroughly enjoyed the excellent
exhibition. When the drill was about half
over quite little excitement was created by
some one crying fire. A break was made for
the street. but when the door was reached it
was found that the janitor had simply lit q
kerosene lamp and the reflection resembled
flames.


A few moments after o'clock Capt. Domer
gave the comu aud to fall in. the roll was
called, and then the work began. The COM
pany was first put through the various foot
movements. and then the manual OF arms.
first by the numbers and then without. For
quite time longer they drilled, and then
Capt. Domer marched them to the north end
of the hall, where the command "Halt' was
given. Here. out of the hearing OF specta-
tors, the commander gave short talk on the
competitive drill He urged them to remem-
Der the city they represented and bring back
the trophy to Washington which they have
won for the past three years.


From present appearances the Emmett
Guard may not go to Little Rock. The COM
pany is short about 900 Of the money neces-
sary to defray expenses, and unless their
friends offer some assistance in the next
twenty-four hours the trip may be abandoned.


The boys have hope that such will not be
the case, and are doing everything possible to
make up the balance. Capt Walsh has not
gwen up all hope, and says II tho money
could be borrowed it would be paid back, as
the company would probably win enough in
prizes to refund.

To brandy peaches you take large
white or yellow free-stone peaches that
are not too ripe. Scald them with boil
ing water, cover and let stand until the
water becomes cold. Repeat this scald-
ing, then take them out, lay them on a
soft cloth, cover them over with another
cloth and let them remain until perfectly
dry. Now put them in stone Jars and
cover with brandy. Tie paper over
the tops OF the jars and let them re-
main in this way one week. Then
make syrup, allowing one pound of
graduated sugar and half-pint of
water to each pound of peaches Boil
and skim the syrup. Then put in the
peaches and simmer until tender. Then
lake the peaches out, drain, and put
them in glass jars. Stand the syrup
aside to cool. When cold mix equal
quantities of this syrup and the brandy
In which you had the peaches. Pour
this over the peaches and seal.

RED BLUFF, Feb. 25-This town has a
fire department which has broken the rec
ord. Not content with extinguishing
blazes that are more or less terrestrial in
their nature they are out in search of
bigger game, and boldly turned the hose
on the aurora borealis. which Illuminated
the northern heavens so brilliantly on the
evening of Washington's birthday.


When the bright red glow was first seen
in the sky by people of Red Bluff, and
while the long rays of light were yet
shooting up toward the zenith some one
turned in an alarm of fire from one of the
electric alarm boxes. In a few seconds
whistles were shrieking. bells wildly ring
ing. and as the boys tackled the hosecarts
and steamers and dashed out into the
street the changing of the gongs added to
the uproar, while the weird ligh. reflected
back from the sSy plainly showed them
that the confiagration was assuming
alarming proportions and urged them to
renewed efforts.


Whirling around a corner and turning
into the main street of the town. running
north, the department made all haste
toward the scene of the fire. but like that
tabled pot of gold which lies buried at the
foot of the rainbow. the light kept reced
ing, and finally as the boys were approach
ing the north end OF the city the light sud-
denly faded and the departments service
was no longer in demand.


The next time that Red Bluffs firemen
are called out to extinguish the aurora
they want some guarantee that the work
will not be completed before they arrive
on the scene.

Milton Shane, of Pablo. was yesterday
morning swimming around outside the surf
and enjoying himself in the water as only an
expert swimmer can. When he was about
600 yards from the beach, floating on his
back he was attacked by shark.


Shane Immediately realized his danger. and
exerted every effort to fight the fish off and
at the same time reach the shore. But the
shark was ferocious and as often as repulsed
would return again to the attack. The young
man, by Observation-Disclosures and bravery, was
able in some degree to evade the monsters
attacks. but not altogether, as at every dash
OF the fish part of the unfortunate swimmers
flesh was torn away. But it was a struggle
for very life. and finally the young man
reached shallow water, and then the beach,
almost exhausted from exertion and loss Of
blood.


1t was found that his thigh bore no less
than twenty-six separate wounds made by the
sharks teeth, which, owing to their peculiar
formation, tore away the flesh at every in
cision. sea captain. who examined Shanes
hurts, said that Judging from the marks the
shark could not have been less than ten feet
long,


Shane's wounds. though many and painful,
are not considered dangerous.-Florida
Times-Union.

A series of interesting tests OF shells
that will penetrate ships having thin armor
and then burst inside was begun at the
Indian Head proving ground yesterday. The
Navy Department contemplates purchasing
several hundred Of these shells for the big
battleships, and for this purpose invited
five firms making shells to submit sam
piles. Two of these, one made by the
Wheeler Sterling Co. and the other by the
Midvale Steel Co., were tried yesterday.
Both were fired with a velocity Of 975 feet
against a seven-inch nickel steel plate, and
both went through the plate and backing
and into the earth. They were recovered
comparatively uniljured. Commodore Samp-
son, chief of the ordnance bureau, says the
test showed that both were excellent pro-
jectiles. The tests will be continued to-
morrow.


Another charge was fired from the Hurst
gun yesterday. The powder charge, lS4
pounds, was the largest yet, and the We
locity the projectile attained was 2,452 feet,
and a maximum pressure of ID $40 tons.
This is about 800 feet greater than the
velocity obtained from an ordinary gun
Of similar caliber, although part of the in
creased velocity, Commodore Sampson says,
may have been due to the fact that the tail
Of the projectile, which weighs about 100
pounds, was broken off. This was the case
with the two projectiles fired from this
gun last week, and the department will
make some steel projectileS before further
tests are conducted.

BUFFALO. Wyo., March 25.-Last weeks
blizzard, continuing seventy hours, has never
been approached in severity by any other
storm in this locality. Traffic is entirely sus-
pended and communication by wire with the
outside world has only just been restored.
Snow is drifted from ten to twenty feet deep in
every direction The mail coach took five days
making one trip from Clearmont. thirty miles.
The loss of stock is terrible. In one herd
near Buffalo containing stock which had been
fed all winter over 20 per cent. perished
The loss of range stock will likely be one
half, which will leave scarcely any stock in
the country this spring.

The engines were at once backed and
simultaneously the sails were clewed up

topgallant yards were sent down, followed

While these duties were being rapidly

ing there terrible exhibition Of prairie

CHEFoo. Nov. %. - Dispatches have
been received here stating that the Japa-
nese captured Port Arthur on Wednesday
last after eighteen hours fighting. The
second Chinese-Japanese army, under the
command of Field Marshal Count Oyama.
Minister of War, consisted of about 80 600
men, and when this force arrived off the
Regents Sword Promontory it was divided
into two detachments, one of which. aided
by part of the Japanese feet. operated
again, Talenwau, while the other di-
rected its movements against Kin Chow,
on the western side of the promontory.
some miles north of Port Arthur. Talien-
wan and Kin Chow were both captured,
after which the army again combined and
the march on Port Arthur was commenced.
Several encounters of minor import tance
took place along the route, but according
10 the reports the Japanese were invaria-
bly, successful.


The roads leading northward from Port
Arthur were supposed TO have been mined
by the Chinese, and the Japanese COM
mands therefore declined to take the risk
of marching along them. Consequently
they were compelled to cut roads through
the forests to allow the passage of their
artillery, ammunition trains. etc. The
march was thus necessarily slow.


Dispatches received few days ago
stated that the Japanese were close to the
city and had attacked the Chinese out
posts. driving them back TO their entrench-
ments. 1t was also said the Japanese at
tackled the enuenchment three times, but
were repulsed each time. 1t is evident
that later attacks must have been made
and that the outUosts were compelled to
fall back upon Port Arthur. Several times
the town is reported to have been cap
tured, but later dispatches have shown
that these reports were inaccurate and
that the japanese were conducting their
operations against the place with great
carefulness.


NEW YORK. Nov. %. - Chefoo, from
which place the dispatch announcing the
fall of Port Arthur is sent, is a Chinese
city on the north coast Of the Shang Tung
PromOntory, some ninety miles south of
Port Arthur, from which it is separated
by the Gulf of Peebili.

NEW YORK, Sept. 16.-Away on old
ocean, with land on either side 1900 miles
away, and on vessel which they believed
to be sinking, was the position in which
the passengers on the steamer Italia found
themselves oD September s.


The Italia did not sink, but came safely
into port to-day with as scared a crew and
passengers as ever were found on ship
board.


That something fatal did not occur
seems marvel, for nothing short of
mlracle made the Italia stand the wear
ana tear of the battle with the waves


When she reached port to-day she pre-
sented only a faint resent blance of the
craft that lett here two months ago for the
Mediterranean.H Most of her lifeboats
were missing and such as were not were
unfit fer use. They were STAYED in and
battered, while the interior of the iron
hulled vessel. at least as far as the pas
sengers' quarters were concerned, was al
most total wreck. The damage was all
due to one wave.


The Italia was not the cnly craft that
had rough passage. The Hindoo, from
Hull, luckily without passengers, had
similar though not quite such a disastrous
experience. She, too, was badly damaged:


Six of the officers and crew of the Italia
were injured Second Officer Chewan was
washed of the starboard ladder and
thrown against ventilator. sustaining
serious bruises. Captain Craigg and
BOatswain Mcfarland we're thrown into
the lee scuppers and when the steamer
rolled were landed against the smoking
room. The captains leg was injured and
the boatswaln received severe internal in
juries. The third engineer was severely
injured about The back and left leg.


On September the storm increased in
fury and at 3 o'clock Captain Craig or
dered the vessel headed toward the sea.
For three hours the passengers were hud-
died together 10 the cabin waiting for what
they supposed to be their last moment.
The steamer rolled from side to side as if
she were going to keel over, while the
voices OF nearly all tie crew could be leard
over the storm repeating the orders from
the bridge. The steering gear had parted
leaving the steamship at the mercy of the
sea. An attempt was made to ship and
man the headgear, but before it could be-
done big wave boarded the steamship
over the port bow and rolled along the
deck, carrying everything before it. Life
boats were smashed and carried away, the
smoking-room aud hospital doors were
burst in and the steam-pTpes on the deck
broken and bent. The chairs screwed to
the floor were torn up, the abin flooded
and considerable other damage done.


The crew, who had been putting the
hand steering gear in place, completed
their work and the ship was once more
headed for port The following day the
storm abated.

SAN FRANCISCO, March 13.-The

his port, Is at Yokohama undergoing
extensive repairs. About a fortnight
ago a cablegram was received here from
Yokohama saying that the vessel had
sailed, but had been obliged to return
for repairs. The steamer Gaelic, which
has arrived from the Orient, brings news
that the damage was very serious.


Two days after the Marion left Yoko-
hama the vessel encountered n terrific
typhoon, which nearly wrecked her.


At one time she was on her beam ends.
A portion of the rigging was carried
away, and heavy seas swept over her.
cutting the Lighthouses and setting
everything on deck awash. The water
poured into the cabins and down into the
engine-rooms.


The boilers were loosened from their
f~astenings. The fires were e~xtinguished
as quickly as possible and the man-of-
war scudded along under bare poles be-
fore the wind. She rode safely through
the storm and sailed back to Yokohama
in a battered condition. The full extent
OF the repairs was not known when the
Gaelic sailed, but 1t is estimated that
she Will be in dock for at least two
months.

TOPEKA, Kan, August g 1894.


The reports from the Cherokee strip coun-
try are exceedingly discouragng and pre-
sent a picture of want and desola ton that
will elicit the sympathy of people every
wehre. The strip of country comprising
the Cherokee outlet Is fifty miles wide and
$50 miles long. With the exception of a
little bottom land skirting the Arkansas
and Canadian rivers, it is almost as barren
as the sandy deserts of Utah Hot winds
which have swept over that country for the
past three weeks, together with the long
protracted drouth, have withered and dried
up every vestige of green, and the 5000
people, who live within the Cherokee strip
boundaries must either leave or suffer the
pangs of hunger.


This is the situation there today. There
is no other Alternative for those who are
still there.


On the 10th of September of last year the
Cherokee strip was opened TO settlement
One hundred thousand people made the
grand rush for homes. On that day blister
ing hot winds from the staked plains of
Texas greeted their incoming. Today the
same destroyer greets the long trains of
covered wagons as they take up their line
of. march for other states where bread can
te secured. 1t is estimated that of the lOO-
600 who went into the strip nearly one
year ago, not more than J0,uU are there





Arkansas, Mississippi, louisiana, Missouri
and other states. Those who have gone
have abandoned their claims to the prairie
dogs and coyotes, the natural Inhabitants
Of that region.


Travelling from Arka nsas City across the
strip to the southwest, one will meet scores
of emigrant wagons filled with men, women
ana children leaving the country. ASK
them where they are going and they can
not tell you. They are fleeing from the
desert. Many are going to southern Mis-
souri, and northern Arkansas, while others
are drifting back to eastern Kansas, where
they have relatives and friends.


Applications by the hundred are being
made to the land ofiice officials for an nd
ditional leave of absence from their home
steads. Under the law the bomesteader
cannot be absent from his claim more than
six months at time. Hundreds are re-
questing an additional three months. 40
they car leave and spend the winter else
where. Then, they say, they will 20 back
In the spring and try II over again. They
still hope that there is an outcome to the
Cherokee strip country, and with a courage
equal to that of the people Of western Kan
sas, who have for years fought against fate.
many will return next spring TO make an
other effort

injury. and that be might possibly patch
up the aperture and return to the Victoria

AS telegraphed to yesterdays Star the
triple screw cruiser Columbia returned to
League Island navy yard yesterday after
noon after a deep sea trial trip that was
extremely gratifying to her officers and
builders.


The following story of the trip is from the
Philadelphia Press: While the details Of
the trip must be retained in secrecy until
the trial board shall have filed their re-
port with the Secretary of the Navy, it may
be said that the cruiser made the fine
speed of eighteen and half knots an hour
under ordinary draught.


1t was reported that she had made twen-
ty-four knots an hour. but this report prob
ably arose from the fact that it is stated
that in burst of speed for half an hour
the vessel made II. 10 knots. Charles H.
Cramp said last night that he could not
imagine that the Columbia could have
made twenty-four knots hour.


The main purpose of the trip was not
to speed the vessel, but to try her machin-
cry and working qualities generally and
therefore no special efforts or preparations
were made Tor speeding her. The record
that she made is the more gratifying on
that account.


The trial was successful in every direc-
ton and confirmed the excellent showing
made by the cruiser at her trial trip last
summer. Three steam trials of six hours
each were made. one under full speed with
natural draught and the three screws work
ing. one with two screws working and the
center screw disconnected, and the third
with the center screw working and the
wing screws disconnected. The test for
coal endurance showed that under speed
of ten knots an hour the Columbia can
steam on thirty-five tons of coal per day,
and going fourteen knots she can steam
with seventy tons per day. The horse
power developed will not be known until in
dicator cards shall have been worked out.


Guns Tested.


During the time the Columbia was at sea
her battery was tested. all the guns were
fired three times. once with a reduced
charge and twice with full service charge.
some slight defects were developed in the
secondary battery. 1t was found also that
openings at the Sponsors were too small.
ara that SUFFICIENT room had not been left
oehind the guns to allow them to be freely
swung when the full gun crew is working
be easily remedied.


Unusual Speed.


With all her fires open and the three nro-
pellers going, she made Il. 10 knots. it was
reported, in thirty minutes Those who
went on the trip are enthusiastic over her
work, and are predicting more remarkable
achievements when she shall go into COM
mission and her new machinery shall get in
smoother working order.


Charles III. Cramp was delighted with the
accomplishments of the cruiser when seen
last night, though, as already remarked. he
did not believe a report that the vessel had
made twenty-four knots could possibly be
correct, and he repeated that the purpose of
the trip was not to speed the vessel at all.


The trial board. of which Commodore
Selfridge is chairman, left for Washington
last night.

directly. 1t depends on family, on race, on
the strain Of that competition which marks
cur advancing civilization. OF these the
two first are ineradicable, though doubtless
capable Of being modified in the course of
generations through judicious marriage.

abnormal excitement, and, even at the sac
rifce of some of the worlds goods, lead
wholesome lives, which would give the
murderous instinct less chance to conquer
them. Physical weakness, especially that
resulting from overstrain, betrays and
weakens the control over the mental flaw.

Company, arrested last night James
Kelley n James Mooney, aged twenty
five and seventeen, respectively, of
Brighton place, Coney Island, charged

adjoining Van Sicklen Station.

went out to see what was the trouble.

facing Sixth street. They had a gray
horse attached to a wagon.


The Waterman notified the Captain,
and he went to Kelley's house. Kelley
was recognized by the Waterman. When
Sarvis reached the house he found Mooney
unloading the wagon.


Mooney told the Captain that ne was
offered Sl.50 to unload the fence from the
wagon. He said he assisted Kelley. but
did not know that the fence was stolen.


Kelley and Mooney were remanded to
Raymond Street Jail for hearing next
Friday.

RHINELANDER, Wis, Oct. S.-Nothing
but unaccountable good luck prevented
the worst passenger wreck of the year on
he $500" Line last night. The Boston,
Minneapolis limited, which leaves here at
1 40 o'clock. went through a trestle be-
tween Heafford Junction and Bradley.
The stringers and piles had been sawed
after ths eastbound limited passed the
place an hour before. The rails were left
with no support and the engine crashed
through. The train was going thirty.five
miles an hour, and instead of dropping
into the opening the engine struck the
solid track beyond and turned over down
the embankment. Engineer James Dutch
of MINNEAPOLIS was thrown twenty feet
ahead. He sustained broken leg, bad
cuts on the head and badly bruised body,
He will recover. He was taken home.
Charles Coterill, the fireman. was pinned
under the heavy engine, which was terri
bly, smashed. UD to noon to-day they
were still working to release his body. He
was instantly killed. He leaves a wife
and two children at Minneapolis.


The baggage-car and sleeper left the
track, but none of the occupants were
badly hurt, The trestle is twenty feet
high,

The grand stand was iammed full and
